key_terms.meaning: For an n×n matrix A, transpose Aᵀ has Aᵀ[i][j] = A[j][i].
Two entries (i,j) and (j,i) with i ≠ j; there are n(n−1)/2 such pairs.
Cost measured by elements read/written or messages sent, not arithmetic operations.
c = Σ_{k=1}^{n} a_k b_k; it is the inner computation of one output cell.
Each C[i][j] can be computed without waiting for any other C[i][j].
Total operations done by all processors together; usually W = p × T_p for time T_p.
Send one value from one processor to all p processors.
Processor i sends to i+1, i+2, ... with distances 1,2,4,...; takes ⌈log₂ p⌉ steps.
For x₁,...,x_n produce y_i = x₁ + ... + x_i (inclusive) or y_i = x₁ + ... + x_{i−1} (exclusive).
A parallel prefix algorithm whose total work is O(n), matching the sequential O(n) work.
Find the k-th smallest element using p processors by splitting candidates among them.
At each step compare the key with p−1 split points and keep one of p subranges.
A device that takes two values and outputs them in sorted order.
Number of comparator layers on the longest path; it is the parallel time.
A sorting network that first makes bitonic sequences and then merges them; depth O(log² n).
A merge network that sorts by alternating odd/even submerges; depth O(log² n).
The diagonal entry used at step k to eliminate entries below it in column k.
Test many intervals or starting points at the same time to locate a root of f(x)=0.
Every component adds its cheapest outgoing edge; chosen edges merge components.
Label each vertex with its connected component by repeated local hooking and merging.

takeaways: Transpose cost is set by moving n² elements, and all n(n−1)/2 off-diagonal pairs can swap at once.
Matrix-product parallel time is one dot product when one processor owns one output cell, while total work stays n³.
Broadcast and prefix sums use doubling to turn p or n items into logarithmically many steps.
Parallel selection and searching cut the candidate range by a factor p per round.
A sorting network's parallel time is its depth; bitonic and odd-even merge networks reach O(log² n) depth.
Gaussian elimination parallelizes the row updates below each pivot, and root finding parallelizes many intervals or starting points.
Graph connectivity and spanning-tree algorithms let many vertices or components choose and merge in the same round.
Always report time, work, and cost, where cost = processors × parallel time.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a parallel algorithm, a step-by-step trace, and a time/work/cost analysis, often comparing PRAM, mesh, and network models.

bank.q: Explain why parallel matrix transpose is a data-movement problem. For an n×n matrix, show that n(n−1)/2 off-diagonal pairs can be swapped simultaneously and state the parallel time with enough processors.
outline: Define Aᵀ[i][j] = A[j][i].
Count off-diagonal pairs: n(n−1)/2.
Each pair is independent; swap all at once.
Ideal PRAM time O(1); realistic cost is data movement O(n²/p).

bank.q: Describe broadcast by doubling and the prefix-sum scan. Derive the number of steps for p processors and n elements.
outline: Doubling distances 1,2,4,... give ⌈log₂ p⌉ steps.
Inclusive prefix y_i = x₁+...+x_i.
Recursive doubling on pairs gives O(log n) steps.
Naive scan work O(n log n); two-level scan can be O(n).

bank.q: Define comparator, compare-exchange, sorting network, and depth. State the depth and comparator count of bitonic and odd-even merge networks.
outline: Comparator outputs two inputs in order.
Network is fixed comparators; depth is longest comparator path.
Bitonic: depth O(log² n), comparators O(n log² n).
Odd-even merge: same order bounds.
Depth is parallel time; comparator count is work.

bank.q: Explain the pivot and row-update step in Gaussian elimination. Why can all rows below the pivot update at the same time?
outline: At step k use A[k][k] as pivot.
For each row i>k update row i using row k.
Updates in different rows are independent.
Parallel time per step O(n) with enough processors; n steps give O(n²) span.

bank.q: For n×n matrix multiplication on p processors with one output cell per processor, derive parallel time, total work, and cost. Compare with the sequential algorithm.
outline: One dot product length n: time O(n).
With p processors, time O(n³/p) if work balanced.
Total work O(n³), same as sequential.
Cost = p × T_p; speedup limited by work and communication.

bank.q: Design a two-level parallel prefix sum for n elements on p processors. Compute time and work, and give the condition for work-optimality.
outline: Each processor sums a block of n/p elements.
Scan the p block sums.
Add block prefix offsets to local elements.
Time O(n/p + log p).
Work O(n + p log p); work-optimal when p log p = O(n).

bank.q: Use p-way search to find a key in a sorted array of n elements. Derive the number of rounds and the speedup over binary search.
outline: Compare with p−1 split points per round.
Keep one of p subranges.
Rounds = ⌈log_p n⌉ = ⌈log₂ n / log₂ p⌉.
Speedup over binary search about log₂ p if comparisons cost O(1).
Mention load balance and communication.

bank.q: Construct a bitonic sorting network for n = 8. Show the comparator layers, total depth, and comparator count.
outline: Build bitonic sequences of length 2,4,8.
Bitonic merge uses log₂ 8 = 3 layers.
Total depth = 3(3+1)/2 = 6 layers.
Comparator count = n/2 × depth = 4×6 = 24.
Trace one input to show sorted output.

bank.q: Describe one parallel Boruvka step for minimum spanning tree. Show how components choose and merge cheapest edges, and analyze rounds.
outline: Each component finds minimum outgoing edge.
All components add their chosen edge.
At least two components merge per round.
Rounds O(log n).
Use union-find or contraction to relabel components.

bank.q: Parallelize Gaussian elimination for an n×n system on p processors. Give the time for forward elimination and back substitution, and state the total work.
outline: Pivot row k is broadcast.
Rows below update in parallel: O(n) work per row.
Elimination span O(n²) with n processors; general time O(n³/p).
Back substitution span O(n²) if each row uses prior results.
Total work O(n³).

bank.q: Compare sorting on a linear array, on a mesh, and on an EREW SIMD PRAM. Discuss parallel time, work, and cost; identify which model gives work-optimal sorting.
outline: Linear array: nearest-neighbor moves; simple schemes need O(n) time and O(n²) work.
Mesh: O(n) or O(√n log n) time depending on algorithm; good locality.
EREW PRAM: O(log n) time with O(n log n) work for parallel merge sort.
Cost = p × T_p; compare with O(n log n) sequential lower bound.
Work-optimal means O(n log n) total work.

bank.q: A program transposes an n×n matrix and then multiplies it by an n×n matrix. Identify communication and computation bottlenecks, and propose a blocked parallel design.
outline: Transpose moves n² elements; multiplication does n³ arithmetic operations.
Unblocked transpose causes scattered memory access.
Blocked transpose improves locality and message size.
Multiplication reuses blocks; one output cell per processor has O(n) dot product.
Report time, work, cost; balance blocks to processors.

bank.q: Compare parallel selection with parallel root finding. Both discard candidates; discuss speedup limits, load balance, and when each is useful.
outline: Selection keeps one of p subranges per round; rounds O(log_p n).
Root finding tests many intervals or starts; independent trials.
Both suffer if one processor has much more work.
Selection has data-dependent partitioning; root finding may need global convergence test.
Speedup bounded by sequential fraction and communication.

bank.q: Explain how parallel connectivity and spanning-tree algorithms use hooking and contraction. Analyze their rounds, work, and cost.
outline: Each vertex or component chooses a neighbor or cheapest edge.
Hooking merges components; at least halving per round.
Contraction builds a smaller graph.
Rounds O(log n) for connectivity and Boruvka MST.
Work depends on edge scanning; cost = p × T_p.

glossary.def: The matrix Aᵀ formed by swapping rows and columns, so Aᵀ[i][j] = A[j][i].
A transpose that uses only O(1) extra matrix space by swapping pairs.
The sum of products Σ a_k b_k of two equal-length vectors.
The total number of basic operations performed by all processors.
The time on an unlimited number of processors, also called critical path length.
Parallel time multiplied by number of processors, compared with sequential time.
Sequential time divided by parallel time, S = T₁ / T_p.
A one-to-all communication that copies one value to every processor.
A scan that turns x₁,...,x_n into all running totals.
A prefix sum where y_i includes x_i.
A prefix sum where y_i includes x₁,...,x_{i−1} but not x_i.
A parallel algorithm whose total work is within a constant factor of the best sequential work.
The problem of finding the k-th smallest item in a set.
Repeatedly halve a sorted range by comparing with its middle element.
A search that splits the range into p parts and keeps one part per round.
A two-input unit that outputs its inputs in nondecreasing order.
A comparator operation that swaps two values if they are out of order.
A fixed wiring of comparators that sorts every input of a given size.
The maximum number of comparator layers from input to output in a network.
A sequence that first increases and then decreases, or can be rotated into that form.
A method that uses row operations to turn a linear system into triangular form.
The nonzero entry used to eliminate other entries in its column.
Solving a triangular system from the last equation upward.
Computing a value x with f(x)=0 for a given function f.
The maximal sets of vertices in which every pair has a path between them.
A spanning tree of a weighted graph whose total edge weight is as small as possible.
